problems.description: For points (x_i, y_i) sorted by x, maximize y_i + y_j + |x_i - x_j| where i < j and x_j - x_i <= k.
hints: Since x_j >= x_i, the equation is (y_i - x_i) + (y_j + x_j).
Keep a monotonic deque of candidate i points keyed by y_i - x_i.
Pop expired candidates where x_j - x_i > k.
problems.approach: For each j, query the best earlier i from a monotonic deque keyed by y_i - x_i, then insert point j.
problems.solution: Maintain a decreasing deque of (x, y - x). For each point j, first expire entries with x < x_j - k, then the front maximizes y_j + x_j + (y_i - x_i). Insert point j and update the answer.

problems.name: Delivering Boxes from Storage to Ports
problems.description: Minimize trips for a truck that carries at most maxBoxes boxes and maxWeight weight between storage and ports.
problems.constraints: Up to 10^5 boxes; port sequence given per box.
hints: Model trips as contiguous segments of boxes.
Dynamic programming over trip boundaries with a monotonic queue for fast minima.
Each segment costs 1 for the storage trip plus port changes.
problems.approach: Use DP where dp[i] is the minimal cost to deliver the first i boxes, optimized with a monotonic queue.
problems.solution: Precompute the running port-change cost and weight prefix sums. Maintain a monotonic deque of candidate split points so each dp[i] is the window minimum of dp[j] + trip_cost. Pop entries that exceed the box or weight limits.

name: Next Greater Element
overview: The next greater element of an index is the nearest element to its right (or in a circular array) with a strictly larger value. A monotonic stack answers all next-greater queries for an array in linear time.
why: Next greater element is the flagship monotonic-stack application and appears in many disguised forms: daily temperatures, stock spans, histogram rectangles, and next greater nodes.
when: Use this technique whenever each element needs its nearest larger or smaller neighbor, especially in a single pass over the array with O(1) amortized work per element.

complexity.time: O(n) because each element is pushed and popped once
complexity.space: O(n) for the stack and result

concepts.name: Strictly greater
concepts.description: The next element must be larger, so equal values do not count as next greater.

concepts.name: Circular wrap
concepts.description: In circular variants, elements after the end wrap around to the start of the array.

concepts.name: Stack of candidates
concepts.description: Pending indices wait in a decreasing stack until a larger value arrives.

concepts.name: Mapping between arrays
concepts.description: Two-array variants look up the next greater for one array's values inside another.

patterns.name: Next greater to the right
patterns.description: Pop smaller indices; the current value is their answer.

patterns.name: Next greater in a circular array
patterns.description: Scan twice so every index sees values that wrap around.

patterns.name: Next greater node in a linked list
patterns.description: Process the list, then resolve the stack with node values.

examples.title: Next greater for every element
examples.problem: Find each element's next greater element in [4, 5, 2, 25].
examples.explanation: 5 is greater than 4, 25 is greater than 5 and 2, and no element is greater than 25.
steps: Scan left to right pushing indices onto a decreasing stack.
At 5, pop 4 and record 5 as its next greater.
Push 2; at 25, pop 2 and then 5, recording 25 for both.
Index of 25 remains, so its answer is -1.

mistakes.mistake: Filling results when pushing instead of when popping.
mistakes.fix: Record an element's next greater at the moment a larger value pops it.

mistakes.mistake: Using non-strict comparison, incorrectly treating equal values as greater.
mistakes.fix: Use < (strictly) to pop, since next greater requires a strictly larger value.

mistakes.mistake: In circular variants, missing the wrap because the scan covers only one pass.
mistakes.fix: Iterate over 2n indices so early elements see later circular values.

problems.name: Next Greater Element I
problems.description: For each value in nums1, find its next greater element in the larger array nums2.
problems.constraints: nums1 is a subset of nums2; all values unique.
hints: Compute next greater for every element of nums2 once.
Map each value to its next greater in a dictionary.
Answer each nums1 value with a lookup.
problems.approach: Run a monotonic stack over nums2 to build a value-to-next-greater map, then answer lookups.
problems.solution: Scan nums2 with a decreasing stack, and when a larger value pops an index, record that value in a dict keyed by the popped element. Map every nums1 entry through the dict, defaulting to -1.

problems.name: Next Greater Element II
problems.description: Return the next greater element for every index in a circular array.
hints: Duplicate the array conceptually by scanning twice.
Process indices modulo n.
Only push each index once.
problems.approach: Scan 2n positions with a monotonic stack, using modulo indices, to cover circular wraps.
problems.solution: Iterate i from 0 to 2n - 1. At index i % n, pop smaller stack entries assigning nums[i % n] as their next greater, then push the index if i < n. Unpopped indices keep -1.

problems.name: Next Greater Element III
problems.description: Given a positive integer n, return the smallest integer with the same digits that is greater than n, or -1 if it exceeds the 32-bit range.
hints: Find the rightmost digit that can be increased.
Swap it with the smallest larger digit to its right.
Sort the suffix ascending.
problems.approach: Use next-permutation logic: locate the pivot, swap with the smallest greater suffix digit, then reverse the suffix.
problems.time: O(d) where d is the digit count
problems.solution: Convert n to a digit list. Find the pivot where digits[i] < digits[i+1]. If none, return -1. Swap the pivot with the smallest greater digit on the right, reverse the suffix, and rebuild the number, returning -1 if it exceeds 2^31 - 1.

problems.name: Next Greater Node In Linked List
problems.description: For each node in a linked list, return the value of the next node that has a strictly larger value.
hints: Convert the list to an array of values.
Use a decreasing stack of indices.
Fill answers at pop time.
problems.approach: Collect node values into an array, then apply the standard monotonic stack scan.
problems.solution: Walk the list to gather values. Scan them with a decreasing stack; when a larger value pops an index, store it as that node's next greater. Indices never popped get 0.

name: Valid Parentheses
overview: Valid-parentheses problems check whether brackets are correctly balanced and nested. A stack is the canonical tool: push openers and match them with closers, rejecting mismatches, premature closes, or leftover openers.
why: Balancing and nesting questions are among the most common warm-ups and appear at every difficulty level, from simple matching to longest valid substring.
when: Use the stack-based approach whenever input consists of delimiters that must be properly nested and closed, or when the problem is a direct variant of balanced strings.

complexity.space: O(n) worst case for the stack

concepts.name: Opener-closer pairing
concepts.description: Each closing bracket must match the most recent unmatched opening bracket.

concepts.name: LIFO matching
concepts.description: The stack top is the only opener that can legally be closed right now.

concepts.name: Immediate failure
concepts.description: A closing bracket with no matching opener, or the wrong type, invalidates the string.

concepts.name: End state
concepts.description: The string is valid only if the stack is empty after the full scan.

patterns.name: Classic matching
patterns.description: Push openers; pop and compare on closers.

patterns.name: Depth tracking
patterns.description: Keep a counter or index stack for the current nesting depth.

patterns.name: Score accumulation
patterns.description: Resolve nested groups into numeric scores with a stack.

examples.title: Validate nested parentheses
examples.problem: Determine whether the string '([{}])' is valid.
examples.explanation: Every closer matches the most recent opener: ')' closes '(', ']' closes '[', '}' closes '{'.
steps: Push '(' then '[' then '{'.
On '}', pop '{' and verify it matches.
On ']', pop '[' and verify it matches.
On ')', pop '(' and verify it matches; stack is empty, so valid.

mistakes.mistake: Using a counter for multiple bracket types, which ignores nesting order.
mistakes.fix: Use a real stack and match each closer against the current top.

mistakes.mistake: Popping from an empty stack when a closer has no opener.
mistakes.fix: Check stack emptiness before popping and reject the string immediately.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the final emptiness check and accepting unclosed openers.
mistakes.fix: Return not stack after the scan so leftover openers invalidate the string.

problems.name: Valid Parentheses
problems.description: Determine whether a string of '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']' is valid.
hints: Push opening brackets onto a stack.
For each closer, verify it matches the stack top.
The string is valid only if the stack ends empty.
problems.approach: Single pass with a stack and a closer-to-opener map.
problems.solution: Map each closer to its opener. For every character, push openers; on a closer, pop and compare, returning false on mismatch or empty stack. Return whether the stack is empty at the end.

problems.name: Longest Valid Parentheses
problems.description: Return the length of the longest valid (well-formed) parentheses substring.
hints: Use a stack holding the index of the last unmatched opener.
Push the index of every '('.
On ')', pop and compute length from the new top or the base index.
problems.approach: Keep a stack of indices with a base sentinel, computing valid substring lengths on each close.
problems.solution: Initialize a stack with -1. For each '(', push its index. For each ')', pop; if the stack empties, push the current index as the new base, else update the best length as i - stack[-1].

problems.name: Minimum Add to Make Parentheses Valid
problems.description: Return the minimum number of insertions needed to make a parentheses string valid.
hints: Track an imbalance counter for open parentheses.
An unmatched ')' with no open '(' requires an insertion.
At the end, the remaining open count is also required.
problems.approach: Count unmatched closers and leftover openers in one pass.
problems.solution: Maintain balance and a required counter. For '(' increment balance; for ')' if balance is zero increment required, else decrement. Return required plus the final balance.

problems.name: Score of Parentheses
problems.description: Compute the score of a balanced parentheses string where '()' is 1 and nested groups double and siblings add.
problems.constraints: 1 to 50 characters; input is always balanced.
hints: Use a stack of running scores.
A leaf '()' adds 1 to the current level.
Nested groups double the inner score.
problems.approach: Push a new level per '(', and resolve scores when ')' arrives.
problems.solution: Start a stack with [0]. On '(', push 0. On ')', pop the level v; the new top gains max(2*v, 1). Return the single remaining score.

problems.name: Generate Parentheses
problems.description: Return all combinations of n well-formed parentheses pairs.
hints: Build strings by adding '(' while opens remain.
Add ')' only when closes exceed opens.
Use backtracking with open and close counters.
problems.approach: Backtrack, choosing '(' or ')' while maintaining the balance invariant.
problems.solution: Recurse with counts of open and close used. Add '(' if open < n, add ')' if close < open, and record the string when both reach n.

name: Expression evaluation
overview: Expression evaluation computes the value of arithmetic strings respecting operator precedence and parentheses. Two stacks (one for values, one for operators) or converting to postfix are the standard engines for these problems.
why: Expression problems test stack discipline, precedence handling, and state management. They range from reverse Polish notation to full calculators with parentheses and unary operators.
when: Reach for an evaluation engine when a problem gives an arithmetic string, asks for a calculator, or needs precedence-aware parsing of operators and operands.

complexity.time: O(n) per pass over the expression

concepts.name: Precedence
concepts.description: Operator priority that decides whether to reduce or continue, e.g. * over +.

concepts.name: Value and operator stacks
concepts.description: Operands accumulate in one stack while pending operators wait in another.

concepts.name: Associativity

def apply(a, b, op):
    if op == '+': return a + b
    if op == '-': return a - b
    if op == '*': return a * b
    return a // b  # truncating division

examples.title: Basic calculator with precedence
examples.problem: Evaluate '3 + 2 * 2' respecting multiplication before addition.
examples.explanation: Multiplication binds tighter, so the expression reduces to 3 + 4, not 5 * 2.
steps: Parse 3 and push it.
Parse +; since the pending stack is empty, wait.
Parse 2 * 2: reduce the product to 4.
Add 3 + 4 to get 7.

mistakes.mistake: Applying operators strictly left to right and ignoring precedence.
mistakes.fix: Reduce pending operators with higher or equal precedence before applying a lower one.

mistakes.mistake: Handling negative numbers as subtraction, losing the sign.
mistakes.fix: Treat a leading '-' as a unary sign by seeding an implicit 0 or attaching the sign to the number.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that a subexpression inside parentheses must reduce before the outer level reads it.
mistakes.fix: On ')', reduce the operator stack until the matching '(' is consumed.

problems.name: Basic Calculator
problems.description: Evaluate a string with integers, +, -, parentheses, and spaces.
problems.constraints: 1 to 3 x 10^5 characters; input is always valid.
hints: Use a stack for values and a running sign.
Parentheses push the current context and restore it after the close.
Treat '-' as flipping the running sign.
problems.approach: Single pass with a stack saving sign and accumulated value around each parenthesis group.
problems.solution: Keep result and sign. On '(' push (result, sign) and reset; on ')' pop and fold the group into the saved result; on digits accumulate the number; on '+' and '-' update the sign. Return the final result.

problems.name: Basic Calculator II
problems.description: Evaluate a string with integers and the operators +, -, *, and / without parentheses.
problems.constraints: 1 to 3 x 10^5 characters; input is always valid.
hints: Defer '+' and '-' while reducing '*' and '/' immediately.
Accumulate the current number before choosing the operator.
Use a stack so additions and subtractions resolve at the end.
problems.approach: Push numbers onto a stack, applying * and / to the stack top as they are parsed.
problems.solution: Track the last operator and current number. On '+' or '-' push signed values; on '*' or '/' replace the stack top by the computed product or quotient. Sum the stack at the end.

problems.name: Expression Add Operators
problems.description: Insert +, -, or * between digits of a number string so the expression evaluates to a target value.
problems.constraints: num up to 10 digits; result must fit in a 32-bit integer.
hints: Backtrack over split points and operators.
Track the running value and the last operand for precedence.
Skip splits that produce numbers with leading zeros.
problems.approach: Depth-first search with the current value and last term so '*' can be undone correctly.
problems.solution: At each position try cutting a number, then branch on operators. For '+' add the term, for '-' subtract it, for '*' replace the last term by last * term. Prune numbers with a leading zero and collect expressions matching the target.

name: Stack & Queue
overview: Stacks and queues are the two fundamental linear containers distinguished only by removal policy: LIFO for stacks and FIFO for queues. Both support O(1) insertion and removal at their access ends and O(n) search.
why: Choosing the right container is a core interview skill. Many problems are simply about recognizing whether nesting (stack) or arrival order (queue) governs the answer.
when: Use a stack for reverse-order, nesting, and undo-style processing; use a queue for order-preserving, arrival-based, and breadth-first processing. Convert between them to satisfy constraints.

concepts.name: LIFO vs FIFO
concepts.description: Stacks remove the newest element; queues remove the oldest.

concepts.name: Access ends
concepts.description: Stack operations happen at the top; queue operations at front and rear.

concepts.name: Container conversion
concepts.description: Two stacks simulate a queue and two queues simulate a stack.

concepts.name: Structural analogues
concepts.description: Stacks mirror recursion and nesting; queues mirror BFS and streaming.

concepts.name: Monotonic variants
concepts.description: Adding ordering invariants to either container enables extremum queries.

patterns.name: Choose by removal order
patterns.description: Pick the container by which element must leave first.
patterns.code:
# stack: newest out first
stack = []; stack.append(x); x = stack.pop()
# queue: oldest out first
from collections import deque
q = deque(); q.append(x); x = q.popleft()

examples.title: Validate a stack sequence
examples.problem: Given a push order and a pop order, determine whether the pop order is achievable.
examples.explanation: Push 1,2,3,4, pop 4, push 5, then pop 5,3,2,1 in sequence.
steps: Push elements one at a time.
After each push, pop while the stack top matches the next target.
Advance the popped pointer on each successful pop.
The sequence is valid if all pops complete.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing a stack where FIFO order is required, corrupting the output order.
mistakes.fix: Ask what must leave first; use a queue for arrival-order processing.

mistakes.mistake: Using a plain list as a queue and calling pop(0), which is O(n).
mistakes.fix: Use collections.deque and popleft() for O(1) front removal.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that both structures need emptiness checks before removal.
mistakes.fix: Guard every pop or popleft with an is-empty verification.

problems.name: Backspace String Compare
problems.description: Given two strings with '#' as a backspace, determine whether they are equal after processing.
problems.constraints: 1 to 200 characters; only lowercase letters and '#'.
hints: Process each string with a stack.
Pop the top on every '#'.
Compare the final stacks.
problems.approach: Build each string's result with a stack that pops on backspaces, then compare.
problems.solution: For each string, iterate characters: append letters, pop when '#' and the stack is non-empty. Compare the two resulting lists.

problems.name: Validate Stack Sequences
problems.description: Given a push order and a candidate pop order, verify whether the pop order is achievable.
problems.constraints: All values unique; pushed and popped have equal length.
hints: Push elements and pop greedily when the top matches.
Use a pointer into the popped array.
Valid if the entire popped order is consumed.
problems.approach: Simulate with a stack, popping whenever the top equals the next required element.
problems.solution: Push each element of pushed; after each push, while the stack top equals popped[j], pop and advance j. Return true only if j reaches the end.

problems.name: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String II
problems.description: Repeatedly remove groups of k identical adjacent letters until none remain.
hints: Store (character, count) pairs in a stack.
Increment the top count for matching letters.
Pop the pair when its count reaches k.
problems.approach: Keep a stack of character-count pairs, collapsing groups of size k.
problems.solution: For each character, if the stack top has the same letter increment its count, else push (char, 1). When a count reaches k, pop the pair. Rebuild the string from the stack.

problems.name: Baseball Game
problems.description: Score a baseball game where 'C' cancels the last score, 'D' doubles it, and '+' adds the last two scores.
hints: Keep a stack of all recorded scores.
Handle each operation by reading the stack top.
Sum the stack at the end.
problems.approach: Simulate the operations with a stack of scores.
problems.solution: For each op: push an integer as is; 'D' pushes 2 * top; '+' pushes top + second-top; 'C' pops the top. Return the sum of the stack.
